candidates.attacker_control: Two vectors. (1) Response side: the fetched host (or any hop in a redirect chain) controls its own Set-Cookie headers, i.e. the cookie names/values parsed by processResponseHeaders() (lines 722-746). (2) Request side: the Location header is server/attacker-controlled; when followRedirects is true (default), each response cookie is copied into req.cookies (lines 531-533) and req is recursively re-executed against the URL resolved from Location (lines 529, 534), so cookies the application intended for the original host are presented to the redirect host.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Checked for any scope handling: Base.cookie()/cookies() (lines 324-349) store only a flat Map<String,String>; getRequestCookieString (813-825) emits all cookies unconditionally; no Domain/Path/Secure comparison exists anywhere in the cookie path; cookies are added before headers in createConnection (638-644). Considered that an application's choice of URL is its own responsibility (SSRF-style argument), but the redirect path forwards cookies implicitly even when the application only supplied the initial URL, which is the cross-boundary behavior. No runtime test was executed to confirm end-to-end behavior.
candidates.impact: Cross-origin cookie disclosure and cookie tossing: cookies established by one origin can be sent to a different, potentially trusted origin, and a hostile origin can inject cookie names/values into requests to another origin. Depending on the application this enables session fixation/overwriting of session cookies, request poisoning, or credential leakage to an attacker-controlled host. Severity is bounded by the application's cookie usage and its exposure to attacker-influenced redirects.
candidates.prerequisites: The embedding application uses Jsoup.connect(...) with cookies it cares about (e.g. a session token) while following redirects (default: followRedirects=true, MAX_REDIRECTS=20), and either the fetched host can redirect to another host or an attacker-influenced host is fetched.
candidates.root_cause: Response cookies are stored in a flat name->value map with no Domain/Path/Secure/HttpOnly processing, and are unconditionally copied into the following request, including the redirect target, without verifying that the cookie's origin host matches the host that will receive it.
candidates.title: HttpConnection forwards response cookies to arbitrary redirect targets without domain/path/Secure checks (cross-origin cookie leakage/injection)
candidates.trace: Response.execute (HttpConnection.java:496-576): on a Location header with followRedirects() true, req.data is cleared and every entry of res.cookies is copied into req.cookies (531-533), then execute(req, res) recurses (534). processResponseHeaders (722-746) parses each Set-Cookie only as name=value up to the first ';' via TokenQueue.chompTo (733-739) and explicitly ignores path/date/domain (comment line 736), so no scope is retained. setupFromConnection also merges previous-response cookies into the current response with no domain check (713-718). createConnection attaches all req.cookies as one Cookie header for every connection (638-642), built by getRequestCookieString (813-825) with no origin filtering; the cookie map also persists on the reusable Request object across later execute() calls.
candidates.unverified: Not runtime-confirmed and not linked to a specific upstream fix or CVE; whether upstream jsoup treats this as a defect versus intended minimal cookie behavior is unknown. Exploitability depends on the embedding application holding valuable cookies and following attacker-influenced redirects; the concrete impact (session fixation vs. disclosure) was not demonstrated.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-565 Reliance on Cookies without Validation and Integrity Checking (also CWE-1004 improper cookie scope/authorization)

summary: Reviewed the assigned snapshot (jsoup 1.8.3-SNAPSHOT; 95 visible files). I traced untrusted-input paths across the parser (Tokeniser/TokeniserState/CharacterReader/HtmlTreeBuilder/HtmlTreeBuilderState/XmlTreeBuilder), the sanitizer (Jsoup.clean -> Parser.parseFragment -> Cleaner -> Whitelist), URL resolution (Node.absUrl), output escaping (Entities.escape/Attribute.html/DataNode), and the HTTP client (HttpConnection). I found no substantiated sanitizer bypass: text is escaped on serialization, raw DataNode output requires the DataNode's parent tag (script/style) to itself be whitelisted and default whitelists exclude those tags, attributes must match an exact whitelisted key, and the URL protocol check rejects values whose resolved/raw form does not start with an allowed protocol. The one concrete, source-verified weakness I can support is in HttpConnection: cookies are stored as a flat name/value map with no scope semantics and are unconditionally forwarded to arbitrary (including different-origin) redirect targets. It is submitted as a lead, not a confirmed vulnerability.
